{"request_id":"9a11b59ea377be5c3820f4da","rewritten_text":"But for me, he never would have gotten out. Morgan le Fay hated him with her whole heart, and she would never have softened toward him. Still, his crime had been done more out of carelessness than out of real wickedness. He had said she had red hair. Well, she did, but that was not a way to talk about it. If someone with red hair is above a certain social rank, the color is called auburn.

Think about it. Among the forty-seven captives, there were five whose names, crimes, and dates of imprisonment were no longer known. One woman and four men—old, bent, wrinkled, and so mentally worn down that they were almost gone. They had long ago forgotten the details themselves. At best, they had only vague ideas, and nothing they could say with certainty. Even the priests who had been responsible for praying with the captives every day and reminding them that God had put them there for some wise reason had only half-remembered stories. They taught patience, humility, and submission to oppression, especially for people of a lower rank, and they had traditions about these poor, ruined old bodies—but nothing more. Those traditions only covered how long the imprisonment had lasted, not what the offenses were. Even with tradition, the only thing that could be proved was that none of the five had seen daylight for thirty-five years. How much longer that darkness had continued was impossible to guess. The king and queen knew nothing about these people, except that they were heirlooms—assets passed down with the throne from the old firm. No history had been handed down with them, so the new owners had treated them as having no value and had felt no interest in them. I said to the queen:

“Then why in the world didn’t you set them free?”

The question was hard to answer. She didn’t know why she hadn’t. It had never even occurred to her. And now she was standing there, predicting the real history of future prisoners at the Castle d’If, without realizing it. It was clear to me then that, with her upbringing, those inherited prisoners were only property—nothing more, nothing less. And when you inherit property, you don’t think to throw it away, even if you don’t care about it.

When I brought my procession of human bats out into the open world, into the glare of the afternoon sun—after first covering their eyes, in kindness, because they had been denied light for so long—they were something to see. Skeletons, scarecrows, goblins, pitiful terrors, each one of them. They were the most proper possible children of Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church."}

{"request_id":"b70f63de12f0710ee92e1bf7","rewritten_text":"But I keep thinking how far you might have gone on, had you been left entirely to yourself. I wonder when you would have spoken, if I had not pressed you to it! My decision to thank you for your kindness to Lydia has certainly had an effect—though, I fear, too much; for what becomes of the moral, if our comfort is drawn from a broken promise? I ought not to have brought the matter up. “This will never do.”

“You needn’t trouble yourself. The moral will be perfectly just. Lady Catherine’s unwarranted efforts to separate us were the very means of clearing away all my doubts. I’m not indebted for my present happiness to your eager wish to show your gratitude. I wasn’t in the mood to wait for an opening of yours. My aunt’s intelligence had given me hope, and I resolved at once to learn everything.”

“Lady Catherine has been of infinite service, which ought to make her content, since she loves to be useful. But tell me—what brought you down to Netherfield? Was it only to ride to Longbourn and be put out of countenance, or did you mean something more serious?”

“My true purpose was to see you, and to judge—if I could—whether I might ever hope to make you love me. What I openly declared, or what I told myself, was to find out whether your sister still had any partiality for Bingley; and if she did, to make the confession to him which I have since made.”

“Will you ever find the courage to tell Lady Catherine what is in store for her?”

“I’m more likely to need time than courage, Elizabeth. Still, it must be done; and if you’ll give me a sheet of paper, it shall be done at once.”

“And if I had not a letter to write myself, I might sit beside you and admire the evenness of your hand, as another young lady once did. But I have an aunt as well, who must not be left longer unattended.”

From her reluctance to admit how much her closeness with Mr. Darcy had been exaggerated, Elizabeth had never yet replied to Mrs. Gardiner’s long letter; but now, having that to communicate which she knew would be most welcome, she was almost ashamed to discover that her uncle and aunt had already lost three days of happiness, and wrote immediately as follows:—

“I would have thanked you sooner, my dear aunt, as I ought to have done, for your long, kind, and satisfactory account of particulars; but, to be honest, I was too vexed to write. You supposed more than really existed. But now, suppose as much as you please; give your fancy free rein, and let your imagination run in every direction the subject will allow. And unless you believe me actually married, you cannot be very far wrong.”"}

{"request_id":"01acc3017d030d47f76933ea","rewritten_text":"It seemed to me that this quaint lie was told in the simplest and most beautiful way. But I had only heard it once, and that makes a difference. It must have been pleasant to the others while it was still new.

Sir Dinadan the Humorist was the first to wake. He soon woke the rest with a practical joke that was, in quality, truly awful. He tied some metal mugs to a dog’s tail and let the dog loose. Then the dog ran in circles around the place, panicked and frantic, while all the other dogs bellowed and chased after him, crashing into anything they could reach. The result was complete chaos—confusion, noise, and a deafening din. Every man and woman in the crowd laughed until they cried. Some even fell out of their chairs and rolled on the floor, delighted. It was just like children.

Sir Dinadan was so proud of what he had done that he couldn’t stop telling the story again and again, to the point of exhaustion, about how the “immortal idea” had come to him. And, as humorists like him always do, he was still laughing at it after everyone else had finished. So worked up was he that he decided to give a speech—naturally, a humorous one. I don’t think I ever heard so many old, worn-out jokes strung together in my life. He was worse than the minstrels, worse than the clown in a circus.

Sitting here thirteen hundred years before I was born, it felt especially sad to hear those same poor, flat, worm-eaten jokes again—jokes that had once given me the dry gripes when I was a boy thirteen hundred years later. It almost convinced me that there is no such thing as a new joke.

Everyone laughed at these old things—but they always do, I had noticed that centuries later. Of course, the scoffer didn’t laugh. I mean the boy. No, he scoffed. There wasn’t anything he wouldn’t scoff at. He said most of Sir Dinadan’s jokes were rotten, and the rest were petrified. I said “petrified” was a good word. I believed that the only proper way to sort the great ages of some of those jokes was by geological periods. But that clever idea hit the boy in a blank spot, because geology hadn’t been invented yet. Still, I made a note of his remark and figured I could educate the commonwealth up to it if I made it through. There’s no point throwing away a good thing just because the market isn’t ready.

Now Sir Kay stood up and started firing at me with his history-mill, using me as fuel."}
